claims.text: Conventional spark-plasma sintering of bare W particles in a Cu matrix typically produces phase separation and voids.
Individual W particles can be given a thin, uniform Cu coating by physical vapor deposition before composite fabrication.
The proposed composite will be spark-plasma sintered in an inert atmosphere at a temperature below the melting point of W but high enough to produce transient liquid Cu.
A Cu coating on W forms a continuous, pre-existing interfacial layer between W and the Cu matrix.
The pre-existing Cu interfacial layer promotes homogeneous fusion with the Cu matrix.
The Cu interfacial layer minimizes interfacial gaps, voids, and phase separation.
Deposited Cu improves the wettability of W by molten Cu during sintering.
The improved wettability results from reducing the interfacial-energy mismatch between W and molten Cu.
An enhanced W–Cu interface produces a more uniform microstructure with fewer voids.
Fewer voids and an enhanced interface improve thermal transport pathways.
An enhanced W–Cu interface improves mechanical load transfer.
The interfacial and microstructural benefits will persist under irradiation stress.
Cu-coated W–Cu made by SPS will have significantly fewer voids than an SPS composite made from uncoated W particles.
Cu-coated W–Cu made by SPS will have higher thermal conductivity than the uncoated SPS baseline.
Cu-coated W–Cu made by SPS will maintain or improve mechanical strength relative to the uncoated SPS baseline.
The proposed performance applies during high thermal flux and neutron irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joints, provided oxidation and contamination are avoided.
The W melting point is approximately 3422 °C.
The optimal Cu-coating thickness has not been established.
The long-term stability of the Cu coating under irradiation has not been established.
